items.title: The brain’s protective barrier also blocks medicine. This engineer wants a way through
items.summary: Rebecca Pinals built a blood-brain barrier on a chip to study how drugs could reach the brains of people with dementia.
items.t: The brain’s protective barrier also blocks medicine. This engineer wants a way through

items.title: Cracks in public health grew in 2026
items.summary: Outbreaks of measles, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and hantavirus exposed a weakened U.S. public health response.
items.t: Cracks in public health grew in 2026

items.title: Timeline: The biggest breakthroughs of the past 70 years
items.summary: For the 70th anniversary of New Scientist, explore our immersive timeline of the biggest moments in science since 1956, from Sputnik 1 to the proliferation of AI chatbots
items.t: Timeline: The biggest breakthroughs of the past 70 years

items.title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
items.summary: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity.
items.t: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

items.title: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
items.summary: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people.
items.t: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

items.title: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.
items.t: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

items.title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why
items.summary: Scientists may have finally explained why up to more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from rocks around the world. New research suggests that powerful currents deep inside the planet slowly raised and lowered entire continents, allowing erosion to erase vast stretches of geological history before they were buried and preserved.
items.t: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

items.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
items.summary: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.
items.t: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

items.title: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert
items.summary: A remarkable 125,000-year-old discovery in Saudi Arabia reveals that early humans once thrived beside enormous lakes filled with wildlife in what is now a vast desert. Thousands of stone tools and ancient plant remains suggest these prehistoric people used sophisticated hunting techniques, potentially including weapons enhanced with poisonous plant compounds.
items.t: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert

items.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
items.summary: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.
items.t: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

items.title: We now know how radiation destroys electronics devices
items.summary: A detailed picture of how a single particle of radiation can destroy a semiconductor device could offer pointers for how to make electronics more resilient to the harsh conditions of space
items.t: We now know how radiation destroys electronics devices

items.title: The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?
items.summary: Data collected since January 2025 show that the measles virus has been circulating for more than a year, a sign that the virus is now endemic.
items.t: The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

items.title: “The gut microbiome will become part of every person’s medical record”
items.summary: As New Scientist turns 70, we asked some of the biggest names in science what the next seven decades will hold. Tim Spector, Jennifer Doudna and more weigh in
items.t: “The gut microbiome will become part of every person’s medical record”

items.title: Just nine countries back pledge to tackle AI’s environmental footprint
items.summary:
The COP31 presidency hopes countries will commit to reducing the environmental impact of AI UN Climate Change/Kiara Worth 

Only nine countries have signed an international pledge to make AI greener, despite warnings at the COP31 climate summit that the technology’s growing energy demands threaten climate goals.

The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge was launched on 16 November at the summit in Turkey. Developed by the summit’s presidency and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), it intends to make AI more sustainable by encouraging cleaner energy use, more efficient data centres and greater transparency about the technology’s environmental footprint.

Read more 
 The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

“AI and other frontier technologies are a double-edged sword,” said Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of UN Climate Change, at a press conference on 16 November. “The task ahead is to blunt their dangerous edges, sharpen their catalytic ones and put these technologies responsibly to work.”

Advertisement 

But Ketan Joshi, an independent analyst researching AI’s climate impacts, questions that analogy. He says it conflates traditional machine learning, already used in applications such as weather forecasting, with energy-intensive generative AI. “You don’t need to have a giant, energy-hungry generative AI chatbot if you want to have better wind forecasting for a wind power developer,” he says.

The initiative comes as AI’s rapid expansion is placing growing pressure on electricity grids. According to the International Energy Agency,…
items.t: Just nine countries back pledge to tackle AI’s environmental footprint

items.title: What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives
items.summary: Scientists and toxicologists are sounding the alarm on the chemicals derived from kratom leaves, which have strong opioid-like properties.
items.t: What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

items.title: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
items.summary: Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.
items.t: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics

items.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
items.summary: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
items.t: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

items.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.
items.t: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

items.title: Plans to rely on carbon removal tech spark debate at COP31
items.summary:
The Climeworks direct air capture facility in Switzerland Walter Bieri/EPA/Shutterstock 

The world is certain to overshoot 1.5°C of global warming. The question now being discussed at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, is whether we can bring temperatures back down again – and what it would take to do so.

If we remove more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere than we emit, global temperatures should eventually begin to fall. The draft negotiating text welcomes efforts to accelerate the development and deployment of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) and carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) technologies. It calls for global carbon capture to be scaled up to at least 500 million tonnes of CO₂ by 2035, with a higher ambition of 1.3 to 2.5 gigatonnes annually, particularly in hard-to-abate sectors.

Read more 
 Can we really reverse global warming after overshooting 1.5°C?

But these technologies have never been deployed at anything approaching that scale, and many environmentalists are concerned that promoting them will undermine efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

Advertisement 

CDR approaches range from planting trees to extracting CO₂ directly from the air and burying it underground . Some involve growing crops that absorb carbon, burning them to produce energy and capturing the resulting emissions . Others aim to increase the amount of CO₂ absorbed by the oceans. CCUS involves technologies that capture CO₂ emissions from industrial facilities and power plants, which can either be used in industrial processes or products or stored underground.

Aakaluk…
items.t: Plans to rely on carbon removal tech spark debate at COP31

items.title: ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site
items.summary: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at the scene of NASA’s historic asteroid collision to uncover what really happened when a spacecraft slammed into Dimorphos in 2022. Its close-up investigation could reveal whether the impact left a crater or reshaped the asteroid entirely, providing crucial clues for protecting Earth from future threats.
items.t: ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site

items.title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way to control exotic quantum behavior.
items.t: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

items.title: What the Trump administration’s focus on AI and quantum means for science
items.summary: Research on AI and quantum science has been favored under Trump, but some scientists are concerned about what it has displaced.
items.t: What the Trump administration’s focus on AI and quantum means for science

items.title: How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096
items.summary:
Fatih Aktas/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images 

How do you invent the future? This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist ’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being New Scientist , I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct.

I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of Terminator alongside the utopia of Star Trek .

I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to population projections , which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are…
items.t: How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096

items.title: Nuclear bomb in space would disable 98 per cent of satellites within a week
items.summary: Just one nuclear explosion in space would have global and long-lasting repercussions, disabling almost every satellite and creating technological chaos from which it would take years to recover, warn experts
items.t: Nuclear bomb in space would disable 98 per cent of satellites within a week

items.title: We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?
items.summary: AI worms aren't real-world threats yet. But tests show they can adapt and spread like octopuses or slime molds, exploiting each device's weaknesses.
items.t: We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

items.title: Massive data centres collectively use as much electricity as an entire US state
items.summary:
Construction work on an AI data centre in Texas covering nearly 40 square kilometres, which will have a capacity of 600 megawatts Backyard Productions/Alamy 

The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to new figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, says Francesca Dominici at Harvard University.

But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information.

Advertisement 

Read more 
 SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike

Together with colleagues, Dominici spent two years pulling together information on 403 hyperscale data centres in the US to estimate their electricity consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions. “Doing these measurements took an enormous amount of work,” she says.

The team estimates that the hyperscale data centres collectively used about 82 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of total US electricity use. This electricity use outstrips the annual power consumption of states such as Missouri, Kentucky and New Jersey. The upper bound…
items.t: Massive data centres collectively use as much electricity as an entire US state

items.title: This is what the world will be like in 2096: A special report from the future
items.summary: In the year 2096, we can talk to sperm whales, we have mostly eradicated Alzheimer's and the synths are developing a base on Mars. But will the non-human people ever forgive us for the damage we have inflicted on our home planet?
items.t: This is what the world will be like in 2096: A special report from the future

items.title: What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing.
items.summary:
Joshua Frieman remembers when the world found out that the universe was made of much more than just matter. For a few years, the scientist had been studying the possibility that the cosmos needed something else — a “missing energy” — to make sense. But it was a niche idea. When he and a colleague started to plan a workshop on the topic in 1997, at first only a few dozen people signed up. Then…

Source
items.t: What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing.

items.title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
items.summary: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.
items.t: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base

items.title: Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy
items.summary: In the largest such study yet, 97 percent of U.S. transgender and gender diverse young people say taking hormone therapy was the right decision.
items.t: Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
items.summary: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.
items.t: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

items.title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
items.summary: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.
items.t: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain

items.title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
items.summary: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.
items.t: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

items.title: The end of the universe could emerge suddenly from nothing
items.summary: A bubble of absolutely nothing – truly empty space – could be out there in the cosmos. Columnist Leah Crane explores how that could exist, and the peril it puts us in
items.t: The end of the universe could emerge suddenly from nothing

items.title: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
items.summary: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.
items.t: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets

items.title: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
items.summary: Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning previous assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.
items.t: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom

items.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
items.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.
items.t: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

items.title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.
items.t: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

items.title: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.
items.t: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study

items.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
items.summary: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.
items.t: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained

items.title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.
items.t: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses

items.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
items.summary: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.
items.t: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

items.title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
items.summary: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.
items.t: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss

items.title: In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck
items.summary: The documentary offers a window into scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean.
items.t: In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

items.title: The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit
items.summary: Infernogallus – the ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur – evolved to eat a fruit-heavy diet. It may be the first evidence of fruit-eating adaptations among non-avian dinosaurs.
items.t: The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit
